Some advice on guitar choice...

  • Don't get an acoustic-electric without adding ~200 to your budget. You don't want to buy a $200 guitar with $150 worth of tech in it that plays like a $50 guitar.

  • Acoustics are harder to set up and maintain so do take care of it, don't store it in an attic or garage, use light acoustic strings. Assuming the neck is straight it's not so easy to adjust the action (without sanding down the bridge) on an acoustic. Definitely try before you buy.

  • Get at least a single cutaway if you want to play lead licks/just for versatility and convenience.

  • Consider the size and shape of the neck (play everything you can afford and maybe some stuff that you can't). It's harder to make clean chords on a tighter spaced board, but it's also easier to do runs and such. Flatter boards are better for bending, more curved boards are better for chords. Some of it will be down to the music you play and some of it to your anatomy.

  • Consider how it sits in your lap if you want to play it on the couch, consider how heavy it is if you want to play it on the stage.

Acoustic is a good first guitar because it will strengthen your fingers quickly, though this can hurt and will require you take more breaks meaning you will learn slower. Depending on your music taste and whether you want to focus entirely on acoustic over riffing, this is the right choice. But i'm going to make the case for an electric anyway.

Electric is good because of the variety of tone available. It's not difficult to get an electric to have a nice clean tone, even acoustic tone is doable these days but to make an acoustic sound like an electric is impossible. Electrics can be plugged into computers onto free software at very low cost, meaning more potential tone/effect options and ease of recordings later down the line, since you wouldn't need a mic/amp/pedals. Lastly, a looper is an invaluable tool for learning the neck and intervals, especially by feel and ear. Great for laying down something simple and improvising with yourself to experiment with musical notes, intervals and patterns; then adding another layer and repeating.

If you have even a little interest in classic rock, learning written solo's or improvisation, go with an electric and maybe a decent small practice amp since I don't suggest figuring out all that computer stuff before actually starting to learn the instrument, you want as plug and play as possible. Schecters and Ibanez are both versatile and play well. Get a Strandberg if you have money to burn. Have fun.
